animals.name: Spider
animals.intro: Lots of people are scared of spiders. Let's get to know one, little by little.

steps.fact: Look at its shadow: eight legs and two body parts. It isn't an insect: it's an arachnid, a cousin of insects.
Spiders have no antennae. To feel the world they use tiny hairs on their legs that sense even moving air.
Almost all spiders are shy: if they see you, they'd rather hide. They only bite if they feel trapped.
A garden spider can eat hundreds of insects a year, like mosquitoes and flies. It's a hunter that helps us!
Look at its eyes: many spiders have eight. And their silk, for how thin it is, is as strong as steel.

animals.finale: You did it! You looked at a spider up close. Remember: look without touching, and if you don't know which one it is, tell an adult.

animals.name: Cockroach
animals.intro: Lots of people find cockroaches gross. Did you know almost all of them live far from houses?

steps.fact: Its shadow: six legs and two very long antennae. It's an insect, a cousin of the praying mantis!
Its antennae are almost as long as its body: it uses them to smell and touch in the dark.
There are thousands of kinds of cockroaches, and almost all live in the forest, under the leaves, turning them into soil.
The few that come into houses are looking for crumbs and water. With a clean kitchen and covered food, they stay away.
Look at its legs: they have little spines that help it run very fast. For its size, it's one of the fastest runners.

animals.finale: Bravo! Cockroaches aren't bad: in the forest they're great recyclers. At home, keeping things clean is enough.

animals.name: Wasp
animals.intro: Wasps can sting, so they're scary. Getting to know them is the best way to stay calm.

steps.fact: Its shadow has a thin waist between the thorax and the abdomen, like an ant's: they're cousins.
Many wasps are yellow and black: it's their way of saying “look at me from far away.”
Wasps only sting to defend themselves or their nest. If one comes close, stay still and calm: it will leave.
Wasps hunt caterpillars and other pests to feed their young: they're garden helpers!
Look up close: clear wings and big eyes. Some wasps also help flowers make seeds.

animals.finale: Very brave! If you see a wasp nest, walk away slowly and tell an adult: that way everyone stays safe.

animals.name: Scorpion
animals.intro: Scorpions are known to be dangerous, and some are. That's why it's good to know them… from a distance.

steps.fact: Its shadow: eight legs, two pincers and a tail with a stinger. It's an arachnid, a cousin of spiders.
It uses its pincers to grab insects to eat. It uses the stinger mostly to defend itself.
Scorpions come out at night and hide by day under rocks, logs… and shoes! That's why we shake shoes before putting them on.
Some scorpions in Venezuela have strong venom. If you see one, move away and tell an adult: never touch it.
A secret: scorpions glow under ultraviolet light! Scientists look for them at night with special flashlights.

animals.finale: You looked up close without really getting close! Respect and distance: that's how you keep yourself and the scorpion safe.

animals.name: Centipede
animals.intro: So many legs moving at once is a bit scary. Let's look at it calmly.

steps.fact: Its shadow is long, made of rings, and each ring has one pair of legs.
It's a myriapod, not an insect. Its name means “a hundred legs,” but it never has exactly a hundred.
It's a night hunter: it eats cockroaches, crickets and other critters. By day it hides in damp places.
Next to its mouth it has venomous claws for hunting. That's why we look at centipedes and don't touch them.
Look at its long antennae: it uses them to find prey in the dark, because it can barely see.

animals.finale: Excellent! Now you know what it's like and how to stay safe: from a distance, and with an adult if it gets into the house.

animals.name: Mosquito
animals.intro: Mosquitoes bite, they're annoying… and they buzz in your ear! Today you'll get to know them better.

steps.fact: Its shadow: very long legs, two wings and a thin beak. It's a fly-family insect, a cousin of houseflies.
Only females bite: they need blood for their eggs to grow. Males drink nectar from flowers.
The buzz is the sound of its wings, which beat hundreds of times every second.
They lay their eggs in still water. If we empty containers with water, far fewer hatch.
Look at its antennae: males have feathery ones, to hear the females' buzz.

animals.finale: Well done! Knowing mosquitoes helps you stay protected: covered water, a mosquito net and repellent when needed.

animals.name: Moth
animals.intro: Some people get scared when a big moth flies into the house at night. Why could that be?

steps.fact: Its shadow looks like a butterfly's: big wings and six legs. Moths are cousins of butterflies.
Its antennae look like little feathers: it uses them to smell flowers and other moths from far away.
It flies at night and lamp light confuses it. That's why it sometimes comes indoors: it's lost, not attacking.
The big dark black witch moth doesn't bring bad luck: it's harmless and doesn't sting or bite.
Look at the dust on its wings: they're tiny scales, like roof tiles. Many moths help flowers at night.

animals.finale: You did it! If a moth comes in, turn off the light inside and leave a window open: it will find its way out.

animals.name: Leafcutter ant
animals.intro: Leafcutter ants bite hard if you bother them. But seen from a distance, they're fascinating little farmers.

steps.fact: Its shadow: six legs, a thin waist and a big head with jaws. It's an ant.
Its jaws are scissors: it uses them to cut almost perfect pieces of leaf.
They work in a line, following a scent trail they leave on the ground. If you step aside, they don't even notice you.
They don't eat the leaves: they use them to grow a fungus in their nest, and the fungus is their food.
Look: a leafcutter ant can carry a piece of leaf much bigger and heavier than itself.

animals.finale: Excellent! Now when you see a line of leafcutter ants, you'll know it's a line of farmers.
